utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Witness. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Sir, I would like to inform you on behalf of the Chamber that you will be testifying today with the benefit of pseudonym, image and voice distortion, this means that there will be no reference to your real name or information which might reveal your identity to the public or media. The audiovisual record of your testimony which is broadcast to the public will have a distorted image, I think we can show it right now, like this, and distorted voice to ensure that your identity is protected and the transcript, while available to the public, will always refer to your pseudonym. Do you understand, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gaynor? Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I please call up 65 ter 90267, which is not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And Mr. Witness, two days ago, did you have the opportunity to review, with the assistance of an interpreter, and with me, a witness statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you make some corrections to that statement and then sign it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you, could you confirm that you see your name and your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you, is that a copy of the first page of the statement which you reviewed and signed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, since you signed that statement, you've informed me of one other clarification which I'll make now for the record. On page 5 at paragraph 23, your statement says that you saw 20 bodies in Drum. Is it correct that you personally observed 10 bodies in Drum on the day of the massacre?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I saw 10 bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection to the qualification. I would ask Mr. Gaynor not to qualify that as a massacre until we see that it actually was a massacre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I thought he was referring to his statement, what -- to what he said in his statement. Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I was referring to the statement which describes the events in Drum as a massacre. I was referring to page 5, paragraph 23.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in the paragraph there is no mention of a massacre, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, elsewhere, it's referred to as a massacre but I take Mr. Karadzic's point. I would like to make one other correction, which is an ERN number which appears on page 10 at paragraph 37, line 3, the ERN number 0101-8994 should read 0101-8984.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, subject to those corrections, do you adopt that statement as your evidence, and if you were asked questions on the same subjects today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I tender the statement under seal, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3262, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll now read, for the benefit of the public, a summary of the statement. The witness gave evidence of the killing by Serb forces of Muslim men in Drum, a Muslim hamlet on the outskirts of Vlasenica town on the 2nd of June, 1992. Serb police came to Drum in late May 1992 and demanded over loudspeakers that the Muslims surrender their weapons. The witness's house in Drum was located on raised ground affording an excellent view of the village. From there, early on the 2nd of June, 1992, he saw heavily armed men lying hidden in the grass and around the village. Upon the arrival of an armoured vehicle, the men broke cover and the witness then saw an extended chain of soldiers emerge from cover. The armoured vehicle went along the road through Drum firing, and the soldiers went from house to house, dragging people out of their houses. The witness describes several incidents where he saw soldiers shooting men in front of their houses with bursts of machine-gun fire. The women, children and old men of the village were ordered to congregate at a particular location. While the surviving villagers were held there under armed guard, a police car came. The driver of the police car was a man known by the nickname Car. The person with Car wore a reserve police uniform and carried a sniper rifle. There was also a military jeep. The villagers were loaded on to a bus amid a barrage of insults relating to their Muslim ethnicity and driven to Susica camp. As the bus left Drum, the witness could see bodies lying around the village of men who had been killed in the attack. He names ten of the victims. At Susica camp, Serb soldiers ordered the Drum villagers off the bus and into a warehouse which was eventually filled with around 1.000 other non-Serbs. For the first days at Susica there was no food. On the third day, men from Vlasenica municipality came to Susica to issue permits to those detainees who agreed to sign a statement saying that they were leaving the municipality voluntarily. About 800 detainees signed such statements, were loaded on to buses and driven away. During that period, the witness also -- the witness saw girls being taken away and returned sometime later. He also saw detainees who appeared to have been beaten, after having been interrogated at the SUP building in Vlasenica. The witness spent 28 days in Susica and was then transferred to Batkovic camp. He was detained there with 1.600 other detainees until he was exchanged on 7 December 1992. That ends the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And now I have just one or two questions for you, Mr. Witness. The first concerns the disarmament of your village before the killing took place. Could you confirm whether weapons were handed in when the Serb police came to your village?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Well, it was just those who had a licence for hunting weapons, nobody else had any weapons. I saw two people handing in the weapons. They took them to the SUP. Nobody else in the village had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want you to take -- take you to the day of the attack itself, the 2nd of June, 1992. Did you at any time, prior to or during the attack, see anyone among your neighbours or among the inhabitants of Drum offer any kind of resistance to the soldiers carrying out the attack?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I have no further questions for the witness. There are no associated exhibits. The Batkovic list which is referred to at page 10 of the witness's statement has been admitted as P3213.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, you will be further asked by the accused, Mr. Radovan Karadzic, in his cross-examination. Are you ready, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness, sir.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, earlier you said that nobody had weapons in Drum other than hunting weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that there was no resistance; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Drum is a village close to Vlasenica, that it's a part of the local commune, the greater local commune of Piskavica, and that it's a Muslim-dominated settlement and local commune?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in your statement, on page 2, paragraph 2, you say that the population of Drum was Muslim with just a few Serbs living in the area, mostly on the outskirts. This is your formulation, mostly on the outskirts, or was that suggested to you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: The first house was a Serbian house and then outside of Drum there were five or six Serbian houses. We were in the middle, closer to Vlasenica than to Piskavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were born in Rovasi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Rovasi and Drum, were they organised militarily before the war, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say that there were no weapons in Drum, would it then be more correct to say that you don't know if there were or weren't, rather than knowing that there weren't any?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One of our previous witnesses, who luckily was not protected here, said that Drum, the Muslims in Drum, were better organised than the Muslims in Vlasenica. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did he speak something that was not true?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Well, you can ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know imam or hodza Munib Ahmetovic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the imam worked to provide weapons to the Muslim people including those in Drum?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you know that there was a Crisis Staff in Drum, a Muslim Crisis Staff, for the entire Vlasenica area and that meetings were held there and weapons were being prepared?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Ferid Hodzic is and where the house of his father is?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I do know Ferid, but I don't know where his father's house is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Ferid was appointed and a self-appointed commander of Muslim paramilitary forces in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was a Patriotic League Green Berets in Vlasenica, that Ferid Hodzic, together with the chief of police, was forming a secret army of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know Tutic, who has a shop in Piskavica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know Hasan Dautovic from Piskavica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far is Piskavica from where you were?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: It's about 400 metres from my house to Piskavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know Nezir Alicevic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And his brother Huso? You said that you saw him get killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know Bego Puric?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Puric Bego from Drum? He lives in Drum? No?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 65 ter 8852 in e-court, please? I'm sorry, can we have 1D4063. 1D4063, please, first, and then we will go back to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a statement of imam Efendi Munib Ahmetovic, the hodza that you knew, and you can see that in this first box it states, in the beginning of 1992, he was summoned, he was approached by the former police station commander, Fadil Turkovic, who was the commander of the police at the time, and offered him Kalashnikovs at a price of 1.500 marks per piece. And then later it says: "In February I was called by Mustafa Imamovic, Zubovic Sahib and Ferid Hodzic, who introduced themselves as the Crisis Staff. We went to Hodzic Ferid's house in Drum, where they asked me to swear and then they offered me to do some work for them about arming the Muslim people. I agreed and we decided," and so on and so forth. Can we look at the next page, please? And, sir, you can see this was on the 23rd of April, the hodza had already told all these things to the police. And then up here, he is explaining to whom he gave those 10 or 11 automatic rifles and rifles, and you can see how many of them are from Drum, Alicevic Nezir, Nezir's neighbour in Drum, he doesn't know his name, it's probably Huso, because we checked, then Hasan in Piskavica, Tutic in Piskavica, and so on and so forth. And you say that they didn't have weapons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I didn't see any. I wasn't really dealing with that. Nobody informed me that they were issuing them or not issuing them, selling them or not selling them. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down a little bit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this is an example how you waste your time. The witness says he doesn't know. There is no point of continuing this part with the witness. You can call other witnesses to rebut the witness's evidence or credibility later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see it. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we get the interpretation. Could you repeat, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. With all due respect, this witness asserts that they didn't have any. I am proving that they did. And his answer is not correct. It would be more correct to say that he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The thing is that you're not proving, you're just arguing with the witness. The witness said he didn't see or he didn't know. Then, that's his answer and you just get on with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement of the 30th of May, 2000, this is 65 ter 8852, on page 2, you say that Serbian families started to evacuate, to flee from Vlasenica, which at that point in time made Vlasenica have a very high Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No. I didn't see any Serbs being moved from Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you upload 8852, and Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Witness, please put a pause between your questions and answers, because both of you are speaking the same language and which have to be translated into either English or French. So, please slow down and put a pause before you start answering or questioning. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are looking for the place, I'm going to tell you how that sounded. It said Serb families began to evacuate from Vlasenica, which made Vlasenica predominantly a Muslim town, and then later you said Muslims also began to evacuate and go to Kladanj. It was very tense, there was a lot of confusion, a lot of stories, and it was impossible to know what the best thing would be to do. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I know that a week before you could get a certificate for those Muslims who wanted to go from Vlasenica from Kladovo. There was no other way to leave. Otherwise, there was a possibility that those who knew could leave through the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Serbian version on page 5, what was just said, and we are now going to look for the part in English. English page 8, with this number. Can you look at paragraph 4. "When the Bosnian Serbs took Zvornik, a month before Vlasenica, we really started to worry as to what will happen to us, because in this uncertainty, people started to leave Vlasenica. Serb families started to evacuate" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I see this exact, almost identical para in para 5 of his amalgamated statement. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict broke out, did both Serb and Muslim families begin to leave Vlasenica and more so the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I didn't see who of the Serbs left. The Muslims were leaving. If they had an approval to go to Kladanj or permission and others went through the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the time before the conflict broke out. Did you not say that the Serbian families were moving out of Vlasenica as it says here, or is this not your statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Well, only if they were leaving on their own, because of the uncertainty. There were more Muslims in Vlasenica municipality but there was no weaponry, nobody was putting up any resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I'm worried about, Witness, sir, is that if the words that are in this statement are yours? Do you stand behind the words? Do you know what you said?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Well, if some Serbs were leaving Vlasenica, they were leaving voluntarily so that they would be safe until they would see what was going on in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you don't remember saying this; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see them leaving. I mean, I don't have anything to remember or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said in your statement of the 6th of July, 1994, on page 1, it's the same number of this but the page has to be somehow different, we will see. You say that the aggression when it was carried out in Vlasenica and so on and so forth, who said that -- who told you that as aggression?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: The aggression was to cleanse all the Muslim people from the municipality of Vlasenica. Young people killed, women and children to camps, and then free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who said that to you, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Well, I don't know their first and last names. I mean, what do you think, that I go and look for them now? I mean, over there, in front of the camp, there were so many people. I was in the hangar. Some people said who went out would never go back, and somebody else said that, well, maybe they will come back in about ten years, I don't know. I didn't see them out there. I just heard their words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you upload Exhibit P3262. But not broadcasting. And why don't you show the witness para 5? We can show the first page first. Sir, this is the witness statement of which you confirmed the veracity with Mr. Gaynor. I show you para 5 of this statement. Do you have a B/C/S version as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The amalgamated statement is only in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I will read it to you. "When Zvornik fell to Bosnian Serbs, a month before Vlasenica, we really started to worry as to what might happen. Because of this uncertainty, people started to leave Vlasenica." And you say, "Serb families started to evacuate out of Vlasenica, becoming a Muslim majority town. Muslims also started to evacuate as well and go to Kladanj." Can you confirm that this is true or this is what you didn't see at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that up until the 16th of April you worked in Bosna Putevi at Sokolac as a guard; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that the Novi Sad Corps came to Vlasenica and you said that they didn't do any harm to anyone.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes. At Drum, no, and I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that in May, the relations between the Muslims and the Serbs in Vlasenica were still good, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further on, you said that in May -- or, rather, in April and May, Serbs asked to have weapons surrendered and they said that nothing would happen to the inhabitants of the villages there, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That happened in the following way. There was a loudspeaker on a vehicle and the driver of that vehicle was a Muslim, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the mentioned hodza was in that same vehicle and that he also appealed that weapons be surrendered and that he took the police to persons to whom he had personally given weapons?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony earlier on -- I don't know whether I can say this actually. 1D4157, pages 7351 and 7352, you said that you had not seen anyone surrender their weapons, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I only saw two hunting guns brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you said that the forces of the Bosnian Serbs attacked the village of Drum?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of June, 1992. And that that was the first attack in that zone and the first village that was cleansed in the operation for all of one month, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, did you see on television or did you know that war in Bosnia started two months before that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No. I just know what happened in Drum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you mentioned yourself that Zvornik happened on the 8th of April, Bijeljina on the 31st of March. You didn't mention that actually but I'm just reminding you of that.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not keep records like that. I just know that until the 1st of June I was fine at home, and as of the 2nd of June, everything cleansed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that an offensive started at 7.00, but at 6.20, and then until 7.00, you were in front of your house and you watched all of that, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that you saw a rather large group of people on the balcony of the Panorama Hotel, you saw them looking at Drum, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the Panorama Hotel, the command of the Territorial Defence was stationed there and, well, also the forces of Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that from Drum, that command was fired at every day, this command that was at the Panorama Hotel?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear yourself that some officer asked a soldier over the radio what kind of bullets were coming from Drum?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No. It wasn't over the radio. When there was this group where we were, men and women, when Car was the first to pass by and then there was a military agree jeep and then this general came up, I don't know, whatever he was, he had these epaulettes, and he asked the first person right next to him he said, "How is the shooting going, how did that bullet reach Panorama?" And he said, "I don't know. Call that person who has a radio. They are up front."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. What is your interpretation of this? How can this officer not know what type of bullet that was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I don't know. Ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In one of your statements, you said that soldiers entered houses, and in another statement, you said that they did not enter houses, or that -- you did not see that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I just saw this cleansing of Drum. They entered houses to see whether there were any men there and then they would take them out and kill them. If they did not find a man, that man would survive because they hadn't seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were not hiding, though? You thought that you were not a member of any political party and that you were not armed and that therefore you were not in any kind of danger; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And I also had no weapons whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. And what do you think, who was in danger?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Well, it depends who came up and what kind of a person that was, whether they let them go, like this woman in a military uniform, she saw me and she said, "Go ahead. There is this group of women in front of Djoga's house." And there was a soldier walking behind her, and she said, "Take him there, because somebody will kill him." And I found about 20 women there, two men. I stopped there and they went on to Piskavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So three men and about 20 women and children were singled out, whereas they went on to Piskavica, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes, there was a total of 28 of us. We boarded buses, the women came from some of the houses there, but there were only the three of us men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the criterion according to which the three of you were singled out whereas they were chasing everybody else?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I found those two on the road there, about 100 metres ahead of me. I don't know how they singled us out. I know that I survived. As for them, I didn't ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is a bit of unclarity involved. From where were you watching all of this that was happening in Drum? Were you sitting in front of your house or were you watching this from your house?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I was in front of the house, in front of the door, outdoors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you're just sitting there in front of your house and there is shooting all over?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I was sitting there, and when the APC came and when they were moving, I did not move anywhere. (redacted) I could not move anyway, but when I saw them taking people out of houses, it wasn't easy for me. I had no idea how I would fare but I mean, whatever, that was my fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At one point you say that you saw soldiers take out Hadzo Malesevic, take him out of his house, and they were shooting?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Right on the steps, that's where he fell, the steps of his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Beforehand you said that some woman called Slavica shot him?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No, no. Slavica is the one who took me prisoner and who told the soldier to take me away. She was above Hadza's house. She walked across my land.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying now, you said in your own statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I have a reference, please, for the earlier evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exactly what I was about to say right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your statement, yes, yes. Actually this is what you stated during your testimony on the 9th of March, 2010, 1D4157, I think. 7358 through 59. Those are the page numbers. I beg your pardon. That's something different. This was the statement of the 6th of July, 1994. That is 8852. 65 ter 8852.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Karadzic could identify the sentence that he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 1 of the Serbian version. Last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we talking about the para which may be identical to para 13 of his amalgamated statement? We'll see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please let us not have this broadcast. I don't actually have the amalgamated statement so it is possible. I have a computer problem so ... page 3 and then it continues on page 4. That's the English version. And that is probably the case in the amalgamated statement as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This section from the 1994 statement is not, in fact, a part of the amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you say that you recognised Slavica Matic and a Romanian from Dragasevac and you say you don't know his name?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes, Dragasevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Slavica was taking Hadzo Malesevic out, and as he was walking down, she killed him with a burst of gunfire. She fired into his back. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I saw a soldier take hajja out and the soldiers who were below the road, below his house, were there, and Slavica was walking below my house, 50 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what you said earlier on, this is actually the 30th of May, 2000, that's not correct, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I know what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this what you were saying? Is this your statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is not correct. Up here it says that the date is the 6th of July, 1994. So what you said then is not correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I know that Slavica took me prisoner and I did not see her kill Hadzo. Enver and Meho fell before she came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. How is it that you don't know the last name of this Omer whose house they also entered?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I don't know. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement of the 30th of May, 2000, on page 3, you say that this was systematic and thorough killing?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who gave you this wording, this formulation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I saw this with my very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does systematic and thorough killing mean in your books?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: It means --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat his entire answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreters couldn't hear you because your answer was overlapped with the interpretation of the question, so could you kindly repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw this with my very own eyes. They were cleansing Drum. All the men were being killed. If people were hiding, and if they managed to hide, they managed to survive. So they cleansed all the men, they killed all the men, and the women and children were taken to camps, towards Kladanj, that's what I saw with my very own eyes. No one said to me, "Go and kill this person or go and kill that person."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, you said this was systematic and thorough killing. Did you offer that wording?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No. It was killing, killing whichever men they found, they killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What's the population of Drum and what's the population of Piskavica, the local commune?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't count them. (redacted) The first house was Rocevic, Serb one, then Roja [phoen]. I did not count the villagers, I worked out in the field, but there were more than 100 houses in that area up to Piskavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in Piskavica itself?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Maybe 50 houses and there were some hamlets, Alihodzici and another hamlet, Brijeg or Brdo, in the direction of Sadici and Durici which were further away from my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you saw that ten people were killed and there were 28 of you on the bus; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you say -- you called this systematic and thorough killing?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where were the Muslim fighters?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where were the other inhabitants out of several thousand?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Slavica kill Meho and Ekrem?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you stated that in one of your statements dated 6th of July, 1994, on page 2?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: There were two men in front of her before -- before she came to Meho's house and this was 50 metres away from where I was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you observed all this. How long did it take, this whole operation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Until they came to me, it took 20 minutes. Everything took place below Hadzo's house. They made this chain from Alihodzici to Vlasenica. The only house they didn't touch was Rocevic, the Serb house. I sat in front of my door. I did see what I did see. I saw five people taken out of their homes and five were killed in front of Nezir's cafe on the plateau. They probably started fleeing but failed. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 2 of this document? You said in your statement that you saw Slavica kill Meho and Ekrem five metres from the house. And now you state that this is not correct.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: There were soldiers there, they were firing. I don't know whether her bullet killed those. There was a soldier entering the house, emerging from the house, then climbing to the first floor, and then took out Meho and Ekrem. And then another soldier came to Fadil's house, took him out. They went from house to house. In those houses where they could see there was no one in there, they would move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Meho's wife and other women joined others on the bus that took you away?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Meho's and Fadil's women, Seka emerged when they were killed and Faketa walked past her husband. Two sons of her and a son-in-law and two brothers-in-law started fleeing and they were killed in front of Nezir's cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A tall soldier told Faketa, "Go to Djoga's [phoen] house"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: In front of Djoga's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the distance between you and those houses?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Fadil's house is ten metres away from mine, and between my ground and Meho's or the fence of Meho is also ten metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the Muslim army in those days had planned and had started a major offensive in different locations around Vlasenica all in preparation of their offensive against Sarajevo on the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that from the 27th of May, attacks had been intensified. For instance, a column of trucks of the bauxite mine was attacked, six drivers were killed. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that they massacred civilians in the Serb village of Metaljka?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Drum was supposed to be the staging post for the attack against Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at 1D01 -- 04068, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll just note this hasn't been listed on the Defence list of cross-examination documents. There is no objection to its use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you explain why it was so, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, we are very few and overloaded with work and this pace of two witnesses per day is exhausting. I'm not tendering this. I just want us to see the situation as reflected here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is dated 31st of May, and the Mirsad Sulejmanovic gives a statement to the police. He stated that he was working as a -- in a warehouse in Skugrici and he describes the attack on the Serb village of Metaljka, involving people from Donja Cerska, Gornja Mahala, et cetera, et cetera, and was carried out on the 2nd June of 1992. And he also says that several people took part in desecrating the tombstones, et cetera, et cetera. Could we please turn to the next page?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Am I supposed to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Did you know that Muslim army activities in that area were daily and intensive?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this is relevant for a subsequent period. Let's leave it. Thank you. Let me read to you a description of those activities so that we can elicit from you whether you knew anything about those. On the 4th of May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. One, whether it's of any point, but you said you are going to read something, a description of something. You need to let us know where you are reading from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the previous page, it says they attacked against the village of Metaljka, the Muslim attack against the village of Metaljka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are reading a passage in Mr. Sulejmanovic's statement? Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We no longer need this document. I'm not going to go very deep into this, Witness. My statement is that this whole area is aflame with activities of the Muslim forces. There are daily attacks against Serb villages. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 27th of May, sabotage against enemy column at Konjevic Polje, enemy suffered great losses, and the communication between the two towns was severed. 27th of May, a sabotage against the power lines. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were power cuts?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes. We thought that you severed the power lines to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then the attack against Redzici, sabotage against enemy forces and vehicles. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 28th of May, attack on Jezica, MTS was captured. 28th of May, Postolje and Prodric [phoen] we drove out the Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's in the area of Birac but in the direction of Konjevic Polje and Cerska?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I never heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Banjevici is located?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 29th of May -- you know where Konjevic Polje is?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 53 Chetniks were killed, and 15 bodies the Serbs could not take out from the area. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 29th of May, offensive against the Kravica, eight Chetniks were killed. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 29th of May, attack of Muslims against the Jasikovaca and Magasici. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Well, they are 40 or 50 kilometres away from Vlasenica. There was no TV broadcast, I did not any news beyond Drum [as interpreted]. I did not have any TV or radio to listen to such news.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Vitorog is?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you how this action in Drum was taken. 2nd of June, in Drum, a sabotage was effected against enemies, that was the headquarters being attacked?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No, there was no shooting when I woke up around 6, and what I saw was a chain of one kilometre from Alihodzici towards Vlasenica. There were no villages there. There was no resistance, there was no shooting, but they scheduled this cleansing of Muslim population for that day. From Drum and beyond, some 1.000 people were brought from Sadici, Alihodzici and the other villages that I did not visit and the -- of course, combat troops went further and they cleansed the area of Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know that this decision was taken?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No. You commanded. You are supposed to know about that decision. You took it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You do not know that a decision was taken. You just surmise?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Well, I know the effect, that there were no Muslims since 1992. I stayed in the area for another month and then went further to Batkovici. I could tell you that there were no Muslims left in Drum or around Drum from that day on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is this passage where you say -- let me read in English, so that it can be interpreted for you. "[In English] The military officer asked the soldier what kind of bullets were coming at Vlasenica from Panorama, to which the soldier answered, 'There is a radio station there. You should find out from them.'" [Interpretation] You said that in your testimony, Stanisic-Zupljanin case, 9th of March, 2010, 1D4157, that would be page 7364 and 7365. Right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I said when the military jeep and the military patrol came in, there was some general there with them. I asked a man in the camp where was that general from? And I got a reply, "From Nis." There was one man who guarded us while we waited for the bus. He -- there was talk about this type of ammunition which flew from Panorama, and the man said, "Ask the man with the radio," and then they moved on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the same Nezir Alicevic? Are there two of them or just one?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I know of one Nezir Alicevic only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is the Nezir that hodza mentions in the context of supplying him with arms and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not engage in such activities. Nobody offered me anything. I did not serve in the JNA. (redacted) (redacted) I could not handle weapons. I was not interested in politics and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were Huso and Nezir brothers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes, brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are their houses adjacent to one another?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So 28 of you were driven to Susica. How many soldiers were there on the bus, as sentries?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Some ten reserve policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So on the bus, there were mainly women, children and elderly men; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: There was a total of 28 of us, and we were the first to enter Susica. When we came there, there was nobody else there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you came to Susica, Susica did not exist thus as a prison but it was getting set up just then?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes, I found ten people down there in front of the door as we were coming out of the bus. The bus couldn't go across the little bridge next to the hangar. There was a small river. There was a small bridge. You couldn't go by car. You had to go by foot. We went out there. We went in there, inside, go in the hangar. We went to the hangar. Nobody was in the hangar. I counted 28 of us, there were a total of 28 of us. Then later by night, people came. There were a thousand of them there. They were being brought from Piskavica, Sanici, Donja Piskavica, I don't know, Bacino Brdo, surrounding area of Vlasenica, people from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In a number of statements, you said that the hall was unprepared, that there were a lot of things in there, that it was dirty, that it needed to be prepared before people could stay there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes. All that was inside were empty shell cases. There was just nothing on the bare floor of the hangar, and we stayed there for a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you helped to clean it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: We just took out the cases. There was no more cleaning done. If you had a coat you took it off and then you sat on the concrete or lie down. Sometimes they would close even the windows, not just the doors, you couldn't breathe. And then after seven to 10 days they brought about 220 people from Papraca. They were in a school somewhere. I asked them. Then they were in the Vlasenica school centre, so they were brought there. They were the first ones to be taken to Batkovici. This is the Kalesija municipality, Osmaci. I don't know those villages where they were from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And these were detainees from the fighting that was up there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I didn't see any of that. I don't know. I just asked those people, "Where were you from," and they said the municipality of Kalesija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. They told you don't worry, you are going to be saved, you will have no problems, you are going to stay here for two days, and then you are going to be exchanged for Serbs from the other side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes. You will be two days in Susica and then you will be exchanged for Serbs in Kladanj. Serbs will come from Kladanj, but this never happened. I spent 28 days and this exchange never happened. On the second or the third day they came from the municipality, the same person who issued permits to leave the municipality of Vlasenica, that you had to go through check-points near Sekovici, I don't know where that was, I didn't go there. From the tunnel towards Kladanj there was a Serb check-point to let you through and that you left on your own to go over there. Well, then, I didn't go anywhere, I didn't pass through anywhere. I didn't ask for the permission. I believed I was an honest man. I didn't dirty my hands anywhere so that's why I stayed. First they said that there were be some exchanges, there were no exchanges, and then after when people were collected to go to Batkovic, they said there was no food in Vlasenica. We went to Batkovic, Sekovljani [phoen] came with us, there was a commander from Montenegro there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And these permits, were they required at the check-point, could you get past with them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't tell you, I don't know what happened to the people, those who went and whether they passed through or not. I didn't go so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you didn't ask for permission, so you weren't given one?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't ask for one, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now that you're talking about the check-points, is it correct that at the outskirts of Drum, before the conflict broke out, the Muslim side held a check-point?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have many more questions, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I haven't even exhausted that hour and I hope I am going to get enough time to ask questions of the witness. All right, I'm going to skip some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were told thus that there wasn't enough food in Vlasenica. Were you told that the Muslim side did not wish to exchange you and that they were asking weapons and food in exchange for you, they were not willing to give up the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: On the bus, when we were leaving Batkovic, this person who is on the bus, they called him Crnogorac, Montenegrin. He had some black suit on him. He had these pockets, two or three grenades in those pockets. He had a kind of jacket, a pistol, I don't know what it's called, it was a bit bigger than a pistol. And he said, "Listen, well, I've brought you here, you have food here as much as you want to eat, there is work, you have to work. And in the morning, we submitted a request to Alija to exchange you for our Serbs, where he caught them. He said, 'I am not giving my own away. Those who surrender to the Serbian forces you can kill them, and in exchange for yours, you can give them some grenades and a sack of flour.' We did not wish to accept that and that's how they brought us here." This is what they told us on the bus when we came to Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that while you were in Susica, very quickly food supplies were established? You were receiving one meal from the military kitchen Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: As far as food was concerned, it was bad. Only food that was left over from the soldiers, that they were delivering to the fighters on the front and that was returned and other leftovers were given to us. Sometimes there was no bread, sometimes there was. But as for food, it was really bad. If we didn't have any people who would send food -- I didn't leave further than the bridge. I mean there was always a couple of loaves of bread, it was homemade bread that was made at home. It wasn't bought. So there was also something like that, but the food was bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this was brought by the neighbouring population; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I don't know where it was brought in from. I don't know, I mean bread was brought in, we would break it up and distribute a piece. Especially those who came from Kalesija, they didn't eat for two days, they were very hungry. They -- we wanted to give them bread. They were more hungry than we were, the local inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this taxi driver, Prlja, is he a Serb or a Muslim? There was a taxi driver, Prlja, who told you, "Give me that gold," so that nobody would kill you for that gold?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did he keep this gold?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your time was up about two minutes ago. It's time for you to conclude. So please conclude before we break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did he keep the gold for you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: I never saw him with my own eyes again. He took it, I didn't see him. After he took it, I didn't see him afterwards, and if I did happen to see him, I would go up to him and tell him, ask him where is that, that and that. As far as I'm concerned, nobody touched me in Susica. In Batkovic nobody touched me either. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: (redacted) As for beatings, I was never beaten by anyone. I would have said had I been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that people freely applied if they wanted to go to Kladanj or Cerska and that most of the women applied and the elderly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes, just to get out of the camp, so that they weren't there any more. They would apply to go anywhere. It doesn't matter. They said there were people in Cerska. They wanted to go to Cerska. I didn't hear it, but all they wanted to do was leave the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Cerska, was that also part of the Vlasenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, it's part of the Vlasenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Some went to Kladanj. The majority of women applied, except some 20 women because they wanted to wait to see what would happen with their daughters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: The bus came in the morning to drive to Kladanj. Ten women said, in the hangar, "We are not going until you return our daughters to us who were taken out in the evening." At about 10.00, two soldiers came and they picked you, you, you, you, you go out. The women asked where are they going. They said that they were going to some old man's place to clean the house, so they were quiet. In the morning when the bus came to drive away, the women stood aside and said, "We are not leaving until they return our children to us." A policeman came, he was Serb policeman from before in the municipality of Vlasenica, I don't know his name. He said, "Mothers, what are you waiting for?" They -- then he went to some little house and in ten minutes, I don't know whom he called, but in ten minutes, these ten girls were back at the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that they did not look as if they were mistreated, that they looked normal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Well, they looked normal. They came to the door, they didn't enter the hangar. They just came and then immediately they entered the bus. I don't know where they went. I don't know if they went to Kladanj or somewhere else. I never wanted to volunteer to ask to leave the camp, doesn't matter where. I wanted to stay in Vlasenica because I didn't do anything wrong to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just have a minute in private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, please, at least until the break because I have to ask about Batkovic. I'm not finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are supposed to take a break at 20 past in regular sitting. And your time was up, but yes, I will allow you put some questions about Batkovic. Conclude in three or four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that in Susica and Batkovic, people applied -- actually reported to work. They were out of the camp in Batkovici for as long as three months. They were taken by one or two guards. They would return fattened, well-fed, and they would bring food back from those jobs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They could report to work and they did not have to report to work; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: These 30 people who went somewhere to Serbia, they were asking for people to build a school. There was a general, he had six soldiers with him from the reserve police, and he told them nicely, "Take these people somewhere to build a school." These carpenters, different kinds of workmen, and tradesmen applied, and he told them, he told them nicely -- I listened in the hangar when he said, "These 30 people you have take care of. If there is shelling you have to catch them in your hands, but nothing can harm these people." And these people were taken in a jeep to this assignment. They were away for three months, and when they came back after three months, each one of them brought 20 to 30 cans of Spam, goulash, all of that looked very nice. They said they didn't do anything. There was a shift, a month and a half, and then another month and a half shift came. They took them to villages, fed them well. They gave them pie to eat. They also gave me food. I didn't go out of the hangar. I'm an invalid, I didn't have to work. They gave me these cans. They gave me cigarettes, 30 boxes of cigarettes, those people especially who didn't smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Other than these 30 people, did many others go for harvesting, to bring in the crops, to cooperatives, and they said that they had it good there and they brought back food?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: Yes, they went out to work every day, because there were about 25 to 30 of us who were disabled, we didn't work. The others did go to work and they would get a meal there, a good one. I don't know what they had, but because I didn't work, I had food that was worse. But they gave me some food as well. I guess they knew me from Vlasenica, so that was why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in Batkovic nobody beat you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-603
utterances.text: No, nobody did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellencies, I believe that I cannot try your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. President, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of this Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. We will rise altogether. Given the pace of the proceedings, the Chamber is minded to take a longer break. Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wanted to advise the Court of a scheduling issue which has arisen. Perhaps we could go into private session, briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. May the Chamber go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor, call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, the next witness is Mr. Suad Dzafic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we include Mr. Mandic, who was a Chamber witness, this witness, Mr. Dzafic, will be the 100th witness in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, he bears that distinction. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzafic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, yesterday did have you an opportunity to review an amalgamated witness statement with the assistance of an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I call up, please, 65 ter 90268.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And you had the opportunity to make some corrections and additional comments to that statement and then you signed it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you, do you see the first page of the statement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you adopt that statement as your evidence and if you were asked questions on the same subjects today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that statement, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3263, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll now read a summary of the statement for the benefit of the public. Mr. Dzafic is from the village of Vitkovici in Bratunac municipality. He returned from Serbia to his home village in March 1992. His statement concerns the Serb takeover of Bratunac town and other villages in the municipality in April and May of 1992. He describes the disarmament of the Muslim population, the destruction of their homes, and their transfer from their villages to places of detention, including the football stadium in Bratunac, the Vuk Karadzic school and the MUP prison in Bratunac town. He was told by Serb soldiers that the SDS leadership in Bratunac had hired paramilitary soldiers to kill as many Muslims as they could. The witness became aware of the killing of more than 60 Muslim villagers in Glogova on 9 May 1992, and the transfer of the surviving villagers to Bratunac. On the 17th of May, 1992, the police chief came to the witness's village and asked the inhabitants to hand in any weapons that they owned. He took four Muslim men to the police station in Bratunac for questioning. On the morning of the following day, 18th of May, 1992, Serb neighbours, armed and in camouflage uniform, and units from the Novi Sad Corps, surrounded the village and informed the villagers that they could not live there any longer. Mr. Dzafic and his fellow Muslim villagers were put onto buses and transferred to the football stadium in Bratunac and later to Vlasenica. Each bus had an armed guard on board. At Vlasenica, the buses were approached by a group of about 30 armed soldiers in full combat gear, some of whom were wearing insignia of Arkan's Tigers and Beli Orlovi and other special units. The military-aged men and five minors were taken to the Vlasenica MUP prison by soldiers. 32 military-aged men and the five minors were detained there until 21st of May, 1992. During this time, they were beaten and maltreated by Serb soldiers. On the 21st of May, the detainees were ordered out of their cell by two police officers and placed on buses where soldiers confiscated their personal belongings including money and documents. The bus headed in the direction of Bratunac, accompanied by an armoured vehicle and four cars. It stopped on the outskirts of the village of Nova Kasaba where the detainees were ordered off the bus by a man known as Makedonac and then executed. The executioners then searched for survivors and shot them in the head. Mr. Dzafic lay on the ground pretending to be dead until the soldiers left. He then fled to Muslim-held territory. Mr. Dzafer discusses a document sent by SJB Milici to CSB Sarajevo which refers to the summary execution of a group of 25 Muslims from Bratunac municipality at Nova Kasaba on 21st of May, 1992. That ends the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, I'll now ask you a couple of questions on some subjects which arise in your statement. I want to take you first of all to the moment when you were taken out of your cell at the Vlasenica MUP prison and placed on a bus. Who placed you on that bus?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: When we got out of the prison cell, we were boarded onto buses. However, an APC appeared, four passenger cars and uniformed soldiers got out of those vehicles. On one of these vehicles, that was a white Lada Niva, there were skulls that were drawn on that vehicle, and also there was an inscription saying, "Bijeli Orlovi, White Eagles." When we boarded the buses, Pero Mitrovic, a neighbour of mine whom I know personally, appeared. He used to work in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I stop you there for a moment, Witness? Who exactly was it that took you from your cell in the Vlasenica MUP prison and brought you onto the bus?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: When we were leaving the prison cell, there were two policemen who came and told us to get out of the cell, stand in a column and leave. There were five minors who they singled out and they stayed behind. As we were getting on to the bus, Makedonac, the Macedonian, that is his nickname, that's what they call him, Makedonac, he walked up to us and ordered us to get everything out of our pockets, money, documents, everything, not to have anything left in our pockets. That is when --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I interrupt for a moment there? Where you said documents, what kind of documents did he instruct you to hand up?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Personal documents. IDs, money, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did anyone explain to you why you had to surrender your identification documents and your personal belongings?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: At that moment no one explained anything. However, on the bus, a man in uniform walked in and said that we would no longer be needing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You describe in your statement the transfer of the bus, transfer of you and your fellow prisoners on the bus until you got to Milici where you stopped. Could you describe what happened when the bus stopped at Milici?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Transfer from Vlasenica to Milici was such that the bus did not stop anywhere. It only stopped in Milici by a tavern. I personally noticed that this Pero was sitting in front of that tavern and there were some policemen there too, in police uniforms. One policeman walked up to the bus from that tavern, he walked up to the front door of the bus and said to that Pero -- I mean it wasn't far away, the tavern and the bus. And he said to Pero, "Let me kill them. Let me finish them off so you don't have to take them any further." And Pero said "No. We are in charge and we are responsible for them." And all of that took a few minutes. And then the bus set out towards Kasaba again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, did any of the Serb policemen at Milici make any attempt to protect you or to negotiate with Pero to secure your protection?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said the bus left Milici and set off towards Kasaba. Could you describe what happened when the bus arrived at Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: When the bus arrived to the entrance into Kasaba, it stopped there. When it stopped, the front door opened. I heard an order to walk out of the back door, groups of four or five men. As soon as that was uttered the back door opened. The first group that sat by the back door walked out. As they were walking out, as they were walking off the bus, as they started walking across a field there, they were shot at immediately. And that's how these groups got out, groups of four or five men. My turn came, I was in the last group. My brother was with me, my cousin, another cousin, and that cousin's relative, Hajrudin, Arif and Galib. As we were by the back door, Galib said to us, "You see, we are walking into our death." I tried to say something to him but no words could come out of my mouth. As I got off, I heard this order to run across the field. At that moment, I just felt something warm going through me, and that's when I fell. All of a sudden, I heard Pero and Makedonac squabbling, saying something like, "We shouldn't be doing this right by the main road." Then, when they noticed that there were people who were still alive, they shot them to make sure that they were dead. My brother lay next to me, so he was alive too. I heard them say, "One of them is showing signs of life." Then I closed my eyes again and I kept silent, because I thought that they had noticed me. However, they came to my brother, they finished him off, they didn't touch me. All of a sudden somebody ordered that they get into the vehicles, the vehicles were ignited, then there was silence. I got up. As I got up, I felt great pain. I started walking across the field, but this pain made me lie down again. Again, I got up. I was in such great pain that I could not even remain lying down. I was bleeding heavily. As I walked across the field, I noticed Ibrahim Muminovic, who was also alive. He said to me, "Suad, I cannot stand on my feet. My legs have been cut off." However, I could not answer anything to that. I continued walking across that field to a river. I crossed the river, trying to save myself. I came across some Muslim houses. However, as I got up and as I walked across the field, fire was opened and they fired at me from a hill that was nearby. However, I went on walking. I didn't know where they were firing from. I just felt these bullets. Not knowing where I was going, I came across these Muslim houses. I was walking on my own for a while, and all of a sudden, Muslims took me in. And took me to the next village. And that's where they --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you for that account. Apart from you, how many other men survived the execution?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Two other men survived the execution, Rahman Karic and Sadam Mujic. However, they are no longer among the living, since the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to what happened to them after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, that ends the examination-in-chief, Mr. President. I have one associated exhibit to tender and that is the MUP document described at paragraph 67 of the statement. The correct 65 ter number for this has been apprised to Your Honours and it is 10772. The 65 ter number which appears in paragraph 53 is erroneous, but I tender 65 ter 10772. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It appears at para 67?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You referred to footnote number. Yes, thank you. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3264, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor. Mr. Dzafic, you will be further asked by the accused, Mr. Karadzic, in his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Dzafic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I need to give you some advice. Because both of you are speaking the same language, could you please put a pause before you start answering the question put by Mr. Karadzic, by the accused, for the benefit of the interpreters and us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wish to express my sympathies and compassion and support to you in view of everything that you've been through. Now I would like us to shed some more light on certain things. You returned to Bratunac from Serbia in March 1992, right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for your return?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: The reason was the following: I worked in Serbia, and on the radio I heard that something was happening in Bosnia. That is to say, I heard that there was some killing in Sarajevo. However, I decided to return to my native town and that's how I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you speaking about the killing of a member of a Serb wedding party in Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: At that moment, I did not know who it was that had been killed. I had just heard that someone had been killed. I didn't realise that it was a Serb who was a member of a wedding party. I didn't know who was killed. I just heard that someone was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How much time had you spent in Serbia until then?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
