utterances.text: About three years. That is to say, it wasn't all of three years without ever going back. I would work and then I'd go back home a bit and then I'd go back again and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you about that because I would like to know whether you were aware of war preparations in the municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Once you arrived, did you find out, because that was a current thing, that an agreement had been reached to transform Bratunac into two municipalities, a Serb and a Muslim municipality respectively?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't all that sure about these two municipalities. I don't really understand that. I heard that they had split up. The MUP, the members of the MUP who were ethnic Serbs got out of the MUP building and they founded their own MUP. As for dividing the municipality into two, no. I didn't know about that. But the split up in the MUP, that did happen. As for the municipality, if that is what you're referring to, then I guess that would be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Muslim MUP remained in the building of the old station, whereas the Serbs, did they establish their own station in the same building or in a different building?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. The Serbs established their own station in a different building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware of the organisation of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets and the arming of Muslims in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On several occasions, you said that there weren't any weapons. However you confirm that your father and another relative had weapons, right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I confirmed that there was no illegal arming. As for the weapons that my father and these relatives and neighbours had, these were weapons for which they had permits. That is to say, pistols and hunting guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement of the 20th of June, 2000, you said that you had heard but not seen that some Serb had killed a Muslim, right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear your answer. Could you repeat it, Mr. Dzafic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that before the JNA came, Mico Stojic and Nedeljko advised you not to go any further than your own houses, not to go into the woods, and also to surrender weapons, if you had any; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was their assessment? What was this danger that existed in the forest?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know. They know. They thought that we were armed, but ultimately it turned out that we had not had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The two persons Mile Stojic and Nedeljko are Serbs from the Serb Territorial Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, these were my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak closer to the microphone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Dzafic, if you answer could you come closer to the microphone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement dated the 15th of June, 1993, to state security in Tuzla, you claimed that your village had already handed in the weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those which were subject to permits, those pistols and hunting guns, this is the weapons I referred to. There were no other weapons. Let us make this clear. The weapons that people possessed with permits for possession of such firearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in your statement from 2000, and I believe it's found its way into the amalgamated statement dated 12th June 2000, paragraphs, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10 and 11, you confirmed that you'd heard about those, that these were not your firsthand information?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Which information?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Information about incidents at the beginning of April, described in paragraphs 5 to 11.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I do not understand at all what you're on about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this means that I'll have to show this statement to you to make clear what I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To wit, if we could retrieve this document, please, 65 ter 20532. Could it be please shown on e-court? The next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think they are identical to the passages in the amalgamated statement, para 5. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, you'd heard that Serbs had taken Zvornik and then you say that the Novi Sad Corps proceeded towards Bratunac or moved on to Bratunac. Did you know that JNA had been deployed in Bosnia long before that and that it had moved from Croatia, from where it had withdrawn, and that they did not come from Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know where they came from. These were Novi Sad Corps members. It made no sense for Novi Sad Corps to be deployed in Bratunac and in Zvornik and in Bosnia. What was the reason for its deployment in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, did you know that the JNA at the time was still the legitimate and the only legitimate military force until the 19th of May?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that, but a corps from Serbia had no cause for coming to Zvornik and Bratunac to establish law and order. There were closer corps that could have done the job. What was the reason for a corps from Novi Sad and Serbia to come all the way to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see that this is important for you. Did you do your national service?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this is important for me, and I asked myself how come that Novi Sad Corps found its way to be deployed in Bratunac and Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where did you do your national service?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: In Cacak. Did you hear? In Cacak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, how come you came to Cacak when you hailed from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, that was still Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A-ha. So on the same basis, Novi Sad Corps could be deployed everywhere throughout Yugoslavia because defence was still unified at the time?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. The Novi Sad Corps was stationed at Novi Sad. If they came from Novi Sad to Bratunac, that means that they were on a mission there. I do understand some things about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify this. Did you know that military districts did not coincide with republican borders?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I did not understand you. Military district borders did not coincide with republican borders?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With republican borders.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the military territorial division in Yugoslavia did not coincide with republican borders? For instance, that one military district could cover the territory of several republics or that in a certain republic you could have several military districts so that military district boundaries did not coincide with borders of republics?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. For instance, the Sarajevo Corps was located at Sarajevo, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And no where else outside Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that. I don't believe. So if Novi Sad Corps was named Novi Sad Corps, they were headquartered at Novi Sad. If the Sarajevo Corps had to come to Novi Sad, it must have been on a mission with a certain task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, the headquarters was in Sarajevo, but its territory went to Slavonski Brod in Croatia and Osmine, Dalmatia, which means that district borders are not the same as republican borders. Do you know that Novi Sad Corps was deeper in Bosnia and that in withdrawing towards Serbia it arrived to Bratunac from the central part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: But what was the task of the Novi Sad Corps in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's leave this subject.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Let's leave this subject. It makes no sense to discuss. Let's discuss what I personally had gone through. Well, what you are saying is important but less important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 of your statement you state that a Serb MUP was established and you say that Muslims were fired from their jobs. Were Muslims fired from the Serb MUP or from the Muslim MUP?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: It could be a slight mistake in this. Muslims stayed on their jobs in the MUPs. Serbs separated from them and established their own Serb MUP. And maybe people working in factories and in municipal bodies who were Muslims were fired. Maybe this is what it refers to. But Serb -- Muslim policemen who worked at the MUP stayed in -- on their jobs and the Serbs separated themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that it was offered for the Muslims to establish their own municipality, so that the clerks and public servants from the municipality could be transferred to the Muslim municipality and the Serb clerks and civil servants could be employed by the Serb municipality?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this is important, Mr. Dzafic, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please slow down and put a pause. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that's important, Mr. Dzafic, when you say that the Muslims were fired, whereas I'm telling you they were not fired. I'm telling you that the Serbs fired themselves from the joint municipality and the Muslims rejected to -- the offer to establish their own municipality. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I was not at those meetings, and I'm -- I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 9 that local Serbs residing in Bratunac joined the paramilitary units. Could you please help us distinguish between JNA reservists, that most Serbs joined, and the paramilitary units, and to describe both, what kind of uniforms they wore, what kind of insignia, and whether any local Serb joined the latter. Do you know that Serbs heeded all reserve JNA mobilisation orders and that the Muslims and the Croats did not heed such orders?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Is your question whether Serbs heeded mobilisation orders and the Muslims and Croats did not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: In which period?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, up to the outbreak of war.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I never -- I was never personally mobilised by anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you arrived to Bosnia, did you know that all Serb able-bodied men were in JNA reserve, although they resided at home but they were part of the reserve JNA forces?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, they went to the combat zones in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They were in reserve, of course they went to the front line in Croatia, but they were there in reserve to be sent wherever they were needed.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Why they were in reserve? What was the threat?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's leave that, Mr. Dzafic.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Let's leave that, Mr. Karadzic. Let's discuss those things that I suffered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will come to that. You discussed these things. I'm discussing what you discussed. You said that local Serbs in Bratunac joined the paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they also reserve JNA personnel?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there a difference between reserve JNA and paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, reserve JNA was there until the military or the JNA came out on the 18th or 19th of May. All of them went into reserve units. Some went to paramilitary units. Some went to Arkan's Tigers, some to White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this is what we want to clarify. Up to the 19th May, the JNA was there and they were reserve JNA as Territorial Defence which was under the jurisdiction of the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Whose Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Each unit of Territorial Defence was under the hierarchy of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Why wasn't I then a member of such Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, you worked in Serbia, so nobody called you.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Why my relatives were not? Why my brothers were not called up? Why none of us were deployed? For what reason? Why wasn't it ethnically mixed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, this is the crux of the matter. They were not called up because they didn't want to, because throughout 1991 and 1992, they rejected any form of cooperation with the JNA. If you're not familiar with that, then I'll have to clarify the matters that you are discussing.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Do you have any documents that anybody rejected such call-ups?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There are plenty, and recommendations of the BH Presidency not to heed the call-up papers. Let's describe those paramilitary units in ways as to distinguish them from reserve JNA.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Listen to me. Let's make this one thing clear. If I worked in Serbia and this is the reason why I was not called up to Territorial Defence, what was the reason why my relatives, cousins and brothers did not receive call-up papers? I would have known that somebody had called them into the Territorial Defence. They would have told me. Let me finish. Most probably irrespective of my work in Serbia, I had to be deployed in Territorial Defence, but I never received any call-up papers. I don't know whose Territorial Defence it was and who organised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see paragraph 9 of your statement, Mr. Dzafic, in front of you? You are saying there that local Serbs in Bratunac joined the paramilitary units. And the question for you was to describe the paramilitaries you said in this paragraph. Was it different from the JNA reservist unit? That was the question. Can you answer the question, Mr. Dzafic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They did -- there were differences between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How could you distinguish them from one another? What kind of uniforms they wore, what kind of insignia they wore?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Reserve JNA personnel were dressed normally in JNA uniforms. The others wore uniforms which were different. They wore insignia of White Eagles or Arkan's Tigers. There were some others. I can't remember all of them. So they wore some insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned skull with a cross bones on a vehicle. Would that insignia correspond to that, what you're --

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the insignia of White Eagles. The vehicle bore that symbol of a skull and criss-crossed bones and then some crosses and the words "White Eagles" was on that white Lada Niva vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And among them, there were few local people, mainly they were not from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: What people are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The paramilitaries, the White Eagles, people wearing those insignia which were other than JNA insignia.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: The people who came to the prison to fetch us, to execute us, well, if you're meaning them, I will explain everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. I'm discussing your time at Bratunac before arrest, before transfer. You said that there were paramilitary formations in Bratunac and that certain Serbs joined them. Was a majority of Serbs in JNA reserve and were the majority of paramilitary units from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: The paramilitary units - I heard people talk - included not only people from the municipality of Bratunac but from all over the place. There were members or people who joined those paramilitary units from the territory of the municipality of Bratunac. Whereas reserve JNA personnel, they were transferred into the Territorial Defence of the Republika Srpska, and you know quite well when this was established and you know that it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that soldiers did not maltreat anybody.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that when the Novi Sad Corps came to the village looking for weapons, they did not maltreat anybody. They treated everybody fairly. One officer was flabbergasted about why they were brought there. They would sit down with us, discuss matters, talked with us at -- a certain amount of time and then went back. And I'm referring to the Novi Sad Corps soldiers who had come to our village to take away the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that they were there for an hour and never maltreated anybody and then went out.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, I cannot be specific about the time but they were fair. They sat down, talked with us, and they were -- they couldn't believe why they were brought there. They were simply confused about why they were there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you said that from the 10th of May onwards, after what happened in Glogova, the Serb Territorial Defence often came to visit your village, more often than before that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And they would stay there briefly and go back, right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, sort of. They would sit and talk to us as well. All these people were our neighbours. I knew them personally. They were not people from elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dusko and Brano came to Vitkovici from Osamsko and told you, that's what you say, that you should escape from the village, and that they would give you a sign when it's safe, that they would fire an M-53 as a sign for you to go back.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: It's correct but what are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I have a reference for that, please, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a statement of Mr. Suad Dzafic of the 15th of June, 1993. I think that I called it up a moment ago. It is 20565. The year is 1993. That is to say, when he got to Muslim-controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that they said to you that you should not separate, that you should stay in the forest, and that they would fire from this M-53, thus giving you a sign that the village is safe and that you can go back.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I want to have it shown here, in Bosnian, in the Bosnian version, so that I see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 20565. That's the 65 ter number, 20565. It is a handwritten document that was typed up. I think it's on page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean, handwritten? This is typewritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a handwritten statement that was later typed up?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: These people took a statement from me. They were typing it up. I probably signed a typewritten statement. Because this is a copy. This is not the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, take a look at what it says here: "Brano Djuric -- Dusko and Brano Djuric, neighbours of ours, who were both between 15 and 17 years old, told us that Milan Djuric said that we should flee from the village into the woods."

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is the way it was. That is what they said to us, that we should flee into the woods seeking shelter, that is to say, while things were happening in Krasan Polje and Glogova. To seek shelter in the forest and they would send us a sign as to when it would be safe to go back to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who was this danger coming from so this Milan Djurkovic told you to seek shelter and that he would let you know who when it would be safe? Who was it that was doing this? Was it these paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. They probably know when or from whom this danger was coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us not have this admitted. I'm going to read it to the end. This is what you say. "The sign for us to return was if Milan Djurkovic opened a short burst of fire from his M-53 light machine-gun, then that would be the sign that we could return to the village. This is what he did. Golub then took us to our village, Dzafici, which had not been torched." Is this Golub a Serb?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he also in the Serb Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then Mijo Stojic and a certain Milan came and another three or four members of the Serb police in uniform, to inform you about what had happened in Krasno Polje. And they told you that Hajran Demirovic, from town, had been killed because he allegedly made rifles by hand. Right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Everything that this statement contains is what I said, and it is correct. We can go on reading it for two hours but this is exactly the way it was. Everything I said was true. There is no need for me to repeat what I had already said. All of that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you said that paramilitary formations then did not take anyone prisoner. After they had received weapons from villagers, right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I am telling you about my village. They didn't take anyone prisoner from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the learned Mr. Gaynor needs this, that is what was said in the trial of President Slobodan Milosevic. I think that it's the transcript of the 27th of June, 2003, and the page is 23236 -- or, rather, 12 through 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further on, you say that the Serb police all the -- from the 10th until the 18th of May patrolled the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: May what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From around the 10th of May, when what happened happened in Glogova. After that they patrolled the village?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say that because of all of that, you began to feel unsafe, and that these same people came and promised that nothing would happen to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Let me clarify that a bit. I felt unsafe, of course. Serbian police, there were no Muslim members of the police force. Well, one had to feel unsafe. And that is true that they did come and tell us that nothing would happen to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you say that they asked for Mehmed Alija Salihovic because he allegedly was training the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that I heard that. Usually they looked for all the more educated, more powerful people. This Mehmed Alija Salihovic was a professor in Bratunac. So all of these people who had senior posts, well, they looked for them, they charged them of being involved with some units, the Green Berets, but I do not even know if there were any Green Berets in Bratunac municipality or that any units were trained. Really, I don't know of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I can accept that, but you don't know that there weren't such things either, right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, as for my village, there were no such things there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you also said that you heard that Mr. Habibovic was killed but that you didn't see that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, could you please repeat that? Which gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Habibovic. I would have to call up the document to see what the first name was. Never mind. Well, I can explain --

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I can explain if we are talking about Fadil Habibovic. It's true that he was taken away and killed. I didn't see it but he was taken away and killed and he hasn't appeared since. He was with me on the bus. He was taken off the bus, brought back, taken off again, and he wasn't seen again. This is if we are talking about Fadil Habibovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this Rahman Karic, was he on some list for having a light machine-gun and that his brother did not hand in his weapons or weapon?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that he was on some list that the Serbs had, that he was charged of having an old machine-gun from World War II. I knew Rahman Karic personally. He was my neighbour. He didn't have one definitely. I mean I'm not sure if he had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And were there any occurrences of Serbs and Muslims crossing the Drina River because of the tensions, because they felt insecure, were they running to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I know Serbs were running away. I don't know if the same applied to Muslims. I don't know if you know of anyone among the Muslims who actually crossed. Perhaps you know that but I personally don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how many Serbs fled, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, they were running away, they would go and they would come back. They would go during the night and return during the day. I heard that from the municipality of Bratunac this happened. Also from my village they would leave in the evening, women and children, and then most of the men actually stayed behind. I'm just telling you about what I know and what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you understand that to mean that there was also fear and insecurity amongst them too?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, probably there was. But I don't know. I'm asking myself for what reason. Well, later, it turned out that there was no danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you say that on the 17th of May, the Territorial Defence surrounded the village and that you were told that you should not go off anywhere from the main road and that nothing would happen to you, and this was told to you by the commission headed by Milomir Babic?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: 17th of May?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know it's 1992. I'm talking about 1992. Yes, on the 17th of May we were informed not to go anywhere, not to run away, that nothing would happen to us. But then on the 18th of May, in the morning, at 9.00, first the electricity was cut, and then information arrived that we had to leave the village, that we can take whatever we could carry with us, to go down to the main road where the buses would be waiting for us. And this is what we did. But when we were leaving, a few people were in the village who informed us, but when we were leaving the houses, I noticed that there were a lot of soldiers coming out of the surrounding woods who continued to loot the homes, to take away the cattle. This happened very shortly after we left. We weren't -- we were hardly on the buses when all of this began. There was firing all around. Nobody was killed. Nobody was wounded. Nobody was mistreated. I must say that. Then when we reached the buses down there, Milan -- well, I don't know if it's Milan. Babic, Milenko Babic, personally I heard him repeat it again: "If you have weapons," still he did not believe, he said, "write it on a piece of paper and hand it in. You don't have to say who had the weapons, just say where they are and there will be no problems." This happened while we were boarding the buses on the 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you told that you could -- they could not protect you unless you all assembled in one place and that you needed to go to the stadium because it would be easier to protect you there?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't tell us that they couldn't protect us. They said, "You're leaving, you have to leave the village." So my village in the Bratunac municipality was the last to be emptied. It wasn't a large village, it's true. The whole village was emptied on the 18th of May, in the municipality of Bratunac. However, people were assembling from other villages who did not leave when people were being expelled from the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, we had a witness here who testified that you were informed to assemble at the stadium so that they could protect you, and that there was no army, no soldiers were escorting you. Did you go by yourselves or were you escorted by soldiers to the bus?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Which witnesses did you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it was a protected witness or not but the Trial Chamber knows this.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, let's just clarify this a bit. I'm talking about my own village. From my own village, no one came to testify. And that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Jasmin Muminovic had some sort of camouflage equipment and that he was taken to Vlasenica for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. This did happen. When we were separated from our families in Vlasenica, from the buses, all the able-bodied men were taken off the bus. They returned a couple of elderly men and they left us able-bodied men including Jasmin Muminovic, who had a rucksack, a kind of bag, multi-coloured bag. They asked him where did he get that from? But he tried to explain that a few days before that, he just came back from serving his term of duty in the JNA and that he brought the uniform and everything with him. But he didn't manage to explain all of that to them because they hit him so much and they took him away to the police station for interrogation at the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you were interrogated about who killed judge Goran Zekic, and if it was correct that you recalled that he was killed on the 8th of May in an ambush when he was going to make some sort of agreement, peace agreement?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I heard that he was killed. I don't remember the exact date. When we were detained in the prison cell, yes, they beat us and they asked us who killed -- who killed him, do you know who killed him? This is the kind of things that they were asking us about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your statement of the 15th of June, 1993, that they beat you for a whole ten minutes, and then someone from the hall ordered the soldiers to stop beating you and to leave the room. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. This happened just when they brought us to prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that local Serbs told you that you needed to just stick it out for a little bit until they got rid of these people from outside and that then you would be safe?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what a policeman or a soldier told us in prison. "If you stick it out and nothing bad happens to you until the end of May," because then he said the mercenaries are the ones who kill and loot, and they need to -- they should be leaving by late May, and then probably after that, you would be safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it correct that later you found out that Jasmin Muminovic was a volunteer in the war in Croatia against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: What? I beg your pardon? I didn't understand the question. Could you please repeat it? Jasmin to have been a volunteer in the Croatian army? No, no. Can you please explain that when you put the question? Are we talking about Jasmin Muminovic? You said that he was a volunteer on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That he participated in the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, you said that he was a volunteer on the Croatian side. That's what you said, if I heard you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were many Muslims from Bratunac who were volunteers on the Croatian side in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but now we are talking about Jasmin Muminovic. How can you say that when the young man had served his military term of duty and was on the side of the Serbs in Croatia? You're saying that he was on the Croat side. I'm asking you, where did you get this information from? Do you have any documents? We can document, all of us can document, on whose side Jasmin was, a member of whose side he was. Until he completed his term of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that your father and brother were taken to Kladanj or Tuzla with a group of women and children, or was it Jasmin's father and brother who were taken away to Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It probably says so in the statement whose brother and whose father. You cannot put questions like that. You cannot induce me to say something that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at page 4 of this document?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I can explain everything but don't lead me to say something that is not true. All the things that I experienced, that I lived through, I'm talking about them and that is true. My truth cannot be denied, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm just trying to understand the situation and I'm trying to show the Trial Chamber what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I'm sure the Trial Chamber understands the situation. You're just trying to provoke me. There is no way that you can manage to provoke me, even if I were here for five nights and five days. What I experienced, Mr. Karadzic, is something that did not ever happen to you for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's look at what it says here. Perhaps you're right. It says somebody came after those who made you sing Chetnik songs left. "After they left, the door was unlocked, and then after 30 minutes, a policeman entered the room where we were locked telling us not to sing and asking us who was Muminovic Jasmin's brother and father. They stood up and they were taken outside of the room, the mentioned policeman in answer to our question said that they would be transported to Novi Sad. However, later, I found out that thanks to Jasmin's participation at the front in Croatia as a member of the JNA, the father and brother were transported to Kladanj and Tuzla, together with a group of women and children." All right, so you are right, he was in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm right and I'm always right, and there is the document. And for sure, had he been a member of the Croatian army, who would have released him? So again I'm telling you, I only am speaking the truth. You cannot induce me to say something that is not true. All I'm going to be doing is telling the truth. And, Mr. Karadzic, don't even try to do that. It's no good. It would be no good. And these questions, I can simply not answer them. I just simply want to talk about things that I personally experienced, what happened to me. As for what I heard and what I saw, perhaps it's important to you. Well, it's important to me as well. But these things that I personally experienced, if you ask me about that, I'm going to answer that, and other things. I don't know if there is any need for any more. Everything has already been told and proved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzafic. Mr. Karadzic, if you have more questions on relevant issues, it's time for you to come to those issues. You have ten minutes to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think everything is relevant your Excellencies so that we can form a picture. The witness is not only talking about the events surrounding the execution. He talks about many other things. This is a part of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that the bus was surrounded by a group of people whom you identified as Arkan's Tigers and the White Eagles; is that correct? The bus where you were on the 18th of May -- actually, the 21st of May.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: The 21st of May in Vlasenica. Let me help you a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh. And what were you told when you were boarded on the buses? Where were you supposed to be going?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: When we came out of the prison, they said that we should be going to be exchanged, or perhaps -- I don't know. But when the bus was going towards Bratunac, I was thinking about all kinds of things. I was even thinking perhaps that they would return us home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what did the policeman tell you, the one who came in, that you were going back home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I have to look. This was 18 years ago. I cannot remember every detail. I'm sure you don't recall every detail either. I can look if you show me where I said that. Let me see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the testimony -- in your testimony in the Krajisnik case on the 11th of February, 2004, at 7 -- at page 748 to page 749, you said that a policeman entered and said that you were going back home.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Where did he enter, to the bus? Into the bus or into the cell?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think he entered the room.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: It's a cell. It's not a room. A room is where you sleep in and a cell is for prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm reading from the English, it says, to the room he told you to come out one by one and to go back home. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's like that, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, when we were coming out of the cell, nobody told us, of course, that we were going to be executed, that we were going to be killed, nothing like that. They said that we were leaving. But I found it a bit suspicious when they separated the five underage young men and left them behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But then you are mentioning some Macedonian from Prilep. Which formation did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I think that he belonged to some kind of sabotage unit from Vukovar. Going by what the people said in the municipality of Bratunac, by the stories there, that Macedonian person killed a lot of people in the Vuk Karadzic hall. I'm just telling you what I heard, I didn't see it. Plenty of people said that. He's from Prilep. His nickname is Makedonac, the Macedonian. Somebody told me and I seem to recollect that, that his name or his last name is Vance [phoen]. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you say after -- in your answer to Mr. Gaynor's question and in your answers, you talk about Serbian soldiers. When you say that, do you mean this Macedonian person as well? Are all of these people Serbian soldiers as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: All of them, of course, all of them, as long as they are killing Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If he is a Serb by ethnicity you call him a Serb soldier?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. I did not say that if he's a Serb he's a soldier. Probably not all Serbs were soldiers. I did not say that all Serbs were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I never mentioned anything like that. I mean, a person cannot remember everything. It's been quite a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Put a question to me. I see that you're not interested in what I've experienced, and your time will be up and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are getting to that, Mr. Witness. So when you say Serb soldiers, was this Macedonian a Serb soldier too?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: This Macedonian was a member of the Vukovar sabotage platoon. Now, if you have information as to who belonged to this Vukovar sabotage platoon, what their ethnicities were, then you know. I'm not quite sure, I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Arkan's men, are they Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Arkan's men, yes. The White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The White Eagles, are they Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have that document that was admitted? I think that's the only one. I think it's 65 ter 10772 but it's already been assigned a P number. It's the last P number. Can we have that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit 3264, P3264.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this, Mr. Dzafic? Do you see that the chief of the public security centre of Sarajevo, the local one, at the time Milici belonged to Sarajevo, or, rather, Sokolac, the seat was at Sokolac, on the 25th of July, the chief asked for information about that particular event. Because it says here, reference here document, highly confidential, number such and such, dated the 25th of July, 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: That is what is written there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On this first page, is there a description of that event that occurred and that you survived?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely. However, there is a small correction to be made. It wasn't 25 men that were killed then. There were 29 who were killed. Whereas 32 were taken out to be executed and 29 were killed and three survived. So this report says that, but there are some things that were not reported on. The report says that Serb policemen tried to stop this group. I don't know whether they did try. I could not notice that they had tried. If they did try, the Serb policemen, then why did this member of the Serb police walk up to the bus and say to Pero Mitrovic, while we were by the tavern, "Let me kill all of them, let's get this done and over with"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This man, did he wear a police uniform and do you know that he is a policeman? Because he's wearing a uniform? Or do you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I did not know him personally. The man was wearing a police uniform, a policeman, a regular policeman, blue police uniform. That's what he was wearing. If all men could wear that, then they are all policemen. I am trying to say that he personally wore a police uniform. I did not know him and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This report, does it mention the same things, the White Eagles, the Vukovar unit, there is no reference to Arkan's men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they have an APC and did they have heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a white APC -- or, rather, a camouflage APC. Over here there is only a reference to one Golf, a red one, Bijeljina registration plates. However, there was another Golf and two Lada Nivas. This other red Golf had Zvornik licence plates, Pero Mitrovic drove that. As for this Lada, I cannot remember its licence plate but it -- one of these Ladas had "Bijeli Orlovi" written on it and the skull that I mentioned as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that what it says here, that at that point in time, the police station had six members that were armed and that this group that had the APC was heavily armed and that they were much stronger?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: That is what is written here, but I cannot understand that a police station has only six men. I mean, I just want to explain this. I did not notice any attempt whatsoever. I did not notice any attempt whatsoever that -- to have things prevented or stopped. If an attempt had been made of that kind -- when we were stopped by that tavern that was very brief. Any kind of attempt to negotiate and to stop people from doing this, that would have had to take time. Whereas this was very fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These men from that group, were they conciliatory or were they cruel?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Which group? The perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The perpetrators, yes.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Were they what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they conciliatory, could you talk to them, or were they arrogant and cruel?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: As far as I am concerned, and what my personal view is, I don't know how I describe these people really. I do not know how to describe them. If I were to describe them here now, it would be ugly for me to speak about what these people were like. But that policeman who wore a uniform, nothing, nothing, nothing, he was no better than them. The one who walked up to this bus, how can he be a good man if he walked up to the bus and said, "Come on, Pero, let me finish them off. You don't have to take them any further." That cannot be a conciliatory man. How can that be a good man?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The time is up. Your last question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Last question, Mr. Dzafic. A moment ago, did we agree that you do not know that he was a policeman except for what you're saying, that he wore a blue uniform?

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: I've explained that. I don't know him personally. He was wearing a uniform, a policeman's uniform. I explained that to you. And that is what I stated, and that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Thank you for your testimony, and please do not feel attacked. I'm not attacking you. I'm seeking the truth.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Karadzic you did not ask me many questions -- I mean, you did not ask me any worthy questions. You did not ask me about these policemen that are on those lists there. Those who beat us in prison, Sladjan Pajic and Goran Gajic, all of these ugly things that happened to me, you barely asked me any questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that in your statement. I am not disputing that, that someone hit you, until I bring witnesses to testify about that. I am not challenging that there was shooting but we have to see who was that was shooting.

utterances.speaker: SUAD DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but then you're saying did anyone beat me, that there is evidence, I have wounds on my body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzafic. Mr. Gaynor, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No re-examination. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Dzafic. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, my colleagues and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you to come to The Hague yet again to give it. Now you are free to go. Please have a safe journey back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness may be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The next witness we will hear in closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next witness will not be testifying today, but he will be appearing in accordance with the protective measures Your Honours ordered which is in closed session, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the next witness will be available now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It depends on his health and we will confirm -- he won't be available to testify today, and we certainly hope he'll be available to testify tomorrow. The second witness for tomorrow should be available also, so we should be able to hear two witnesses tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your suggestion is to hear the evidence of those two tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- not today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then we are -- before we adjourn for today, I would like to issue an oral ruling in relation to the status of the "Request for International Legal Assistance in Hearing Witnesses via Video Conference Link," filed confidentially and ex parte on the 1st of August, 2011, by the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The ex parte status was lifted by the order of the duty judge of 2nd of August, 2011. In his submission dated 4th of August, 2011, the accused requested, inter alia, that the matter be reclassified as public. In its "Decision on Request for Assistance of the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina Pursuant to Rule 75 bis," issued confidentially on 9 August 2011, the Chamber invited the BiH court to indicate why the request should remain confidential. The Chamber has now been informed by the BiH Court that the Court did not intend for its request to be regarded as a confidential submission. In light of this, the Chamber orders that confidentiality be lifted on the following, and that each reclassified as public. 1: The Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina's "Request for International Legal Assistance in Hearing Witnesses via Video Conference Link," filed on 1st of August, 2011. 2: The "Prosecution's Response to Confidential Request for Assistance," filed on 3rd of August, 2011. 3: The accused's submission, entitled, "Submission of Radovan Karadzic," filed on 4th of August, 2011. 4: The Chamber's "Decision on Request for Assistance of the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina Pursuant to Rule 75 bis," issued on 9th of August, 2011. Unless there are other matters to be raised, we will adjourn for today. Tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
